newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--NYMEX crude craters on vague Saudi report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--NYMEX crude craters on vague Saudi report.

text.p: NYMEX oil prices cratered just before the close Monday on a report--denied by U.S. and Mideast Gulf sources--that the U.S. had requested Saudi crude production increases.
"It was definitely that Saudi story. It is kind of a bogus story," said Tom Bentz, oil market analyst at ING Derivatives.

Oil traders said the story suggested the U.S. would ask Saudis to raise production to offset the fact that the UN-Iraq oil-for-food deal was postponed due to the latest U.S.-Iraqi tensions. Crude oil for October delivery ended $1.32 lower at $23.19 a barrel, with most of the loss linked to the report.
"Saudi Arabia is currently sticking to its quota and will not change it except within OPEC," a Gulf source told Reuters.

"We let the free market run its course in terms of supply and demand," said a U.S. State Department official, when asked whether the United States had asked Saudi Arabia to increase its output to make up for the delay in Iraqi exports.
Refined product prices on the NYMEX were also dragged down in the closing minutes of the session.
Heating oil for October delivery shed 2.65 cents and settled at 65.29 cents a gallon, while October gasoline lost 1.73 cents and ended at 62.87 cents a gallon.

Traders said the bogus story perhaps served to bring prices to lower levels to which they were gravitating anyway, since oil traders have begun to increasingly view recent tensions between the U.S. and Iraq as declining.

"We basically just gave up the Iraqi quotient," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil, noting the intraday high of October crude late last month before U.S.-Iraq tensions flared was just above Monday's low.
Incursions by Iraqi troops into Kurdish zones in the north of the country led to U.S. missile strikes early this month as well as the expansion of Allied-enforced "no-fly" zones for Iraqi warplanes.
Monday's session low on October crude was $23.10.
"The downside looked like it would be back at $23, and that's exactly where we are," said ING's Bentz.
Still sources said that oil markets are likely to remain strong given low heating oil stocks.

"The heating oil fundamentals are strong," said Thomas Blakeslee, of Cargill Investor Services, referring to industry data showing heating oil stocks at just 48.4 million barrels or more than 19 million barrels below year-ago levels.
Even the U.S. Energy Department raised a warning flag Monday, saying stocks were now so low as to make higher prices -- if not severe price spikes -- a real possibility this winter.
-- Oliver Ludwig, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1620
